updates.issuing_body: Sejm of the Republic of Poland
updates.summary: Poland's law implementing the EU AI Act. It creates the Commission for the Development and Security of Artificial Intelligence (KRiBSI) as market surveillance authority and single point of contact: a chair, two deputies and four members nominated by the competition, financial, broadcasting and electronic communications regulators, independent in their functions. The Commission inspects compliance, handles complaints, issues warnings and binding individual opinions, can order an AI system that poses a direct risk to life, health, safety or fundamental rights to be withdrawn from the market or from use, imposes the AI Act's fines and runs a regulatory sandbox, free for SMEs.
updates.notes: Published in the Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw) on 27 July 2026 as item 1003, with the signature of President Nawrocki. The Act entered into force 14 days after publication, on 11 August 2026; Article 125(4), on setting up the unit of the digital affairs ministry that serves the Commission, applied from 28 July 2026. Articles 8 to 18 (individual opinions and explanations) and Chapters 3 to 5 (inspections, proceedings, settlements on mitigating sanctions), 8 (administrative fines and criminal provisions) and 9 (amendments to ten other acts) apply from 28 October 2026, three months after publication. The minister responsible for digital affairs (informatisation) is the notifying authority. The Sejm, with the Senate's consent, appoints the Commission's chair within two months of entry into force, and the chair convenes the first meeting within three months. A Social Council for AI of 9 to 15 members advises the Commission. The Act caps state spending on it at PLN 9.30 million in 2026, rising to PLN 29.68 million in 2035.

updates.summary: Presidential decree approving Russia's National Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence to 2030, which federal executive bodies must follow. Its binding principles include protection of human rights and freedoms, safety (no use of AI to deliberately harm people, minimising the risk of negative consequences) and transparency. The 2024 revision defines large generative and foundation models and trusted AI technologies and adds rules for regulating AI: a risk-based approach, non-discrimination, respect for human autonomy, liability always resting with a natural or legal person, information-security requirements, and certification of AI solutions used by federal bodies.
updates.notes: In force from signature on 10 October 2019. Decree No. 124 of 15 February 2024 revised both the decree and the Strategy: it added definitions of large generative models, large foundation models (at least 1 billion parameters), strong AI and trusted AI technologies, a new section on the regulation of AI and the safety of its use, the mandatory use of trusted AI technologies where harm to the security of the Russian Federation is possible, and a register of trusted AI technologies tested against information-security threats; it also required federal executive bodies to follow the Strategy, recommended that regional and local authorities do the same, and asked state corporations and companies with state participation to add AI development measures to their strategies by 1 November 2024. The Strategy notes that creating universal ('strong') AI could have negative consequences. The English translation listed covers the 2019 text, before the 2024 amendments.
updates.scope_note: Mainly a development strategy; its safety content is a set of principles and, since 2024, a section on regulation and the safety of AI. Included as Russia's national AI strategy, which federal executive bodies must follow.

updates.summary: Amendment to Croatia's Criminal Code, adopted on 24 October 2025, that adds the AI Act's definition of an AI system (Article 87(33)) and a new offence, Article 215.a 'Endangering life and property by an artificial intelligence system'. Whoever, in the development, testing, verification, supervision, management or use of an AI system, or otherwise by means of one, causes danger to human life or body or to large-scale property faces six months to five years' imprisonment, or up to three years if negligent. Serious bodily injury or large-scale damage raises this to one to ten years (six months to five if negligent), death to three to fifteen years (one to eight if negligent).

Article 215.a applies only where no more serious criminal offence is committed. updates.summary: Private members' bill by SOS România senators and deputies that would regulate AI use in Romania. updates.summary: Private members' bill that would apply Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and govern AI in the public sector, AI skills, investment and AI risks to national security and children. It splits market surveillance among sector regulators, makes the Minister of Innovation and Digital Transformation the notifying authority and the Communications Regulation Commission the single point of contact. It bans remote biometric identification and the AI Act's prohibited practices, prohibits publishing convincing AI fakes of senior officials, or of others without consent, with removal orders, bars training models on children's data save narrow exceptions with parental consent, and sets fines up to BGN 5 million.
updates.notes: Filed on 24 September 2026 by ten members of the 52nd National Assembly, led by Bozhidar Bozhanov, and distributed on 25 September 2026 (order 52-650-01-318) to the Committee on Innovation and Digital Transformation as lead committee and to sixteen other committees. By 17 October 2026 no committee report for first reading was listed; opinions had been filed by, among others, the Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation and the State Agency for National Security (15 October 2026). The bill would enter into force two months after promulgation, except Article 22, § 7 and § 21, from 1 July 2027. It would also create a national AI coordinator appointed by the Prime Minister, an advisory council at the Council of Ministers and an AI regulatory sandbox, require AI systems that the Council of Ministers designates as high-risk for national security, such as recommender systems of very large online platforms, to give the State Agency for National Security and the ministry their source code, documentation and a description of their training data, and amend the Criminal Code (AI-generated pornographic content), the Election Code (labelling of campaign material made with AI) and the Judiciary Act (courts may not use AI to interpret facts and law).
updates.scope_note: Private members' bill by opposition MPs; included because it is the fullest bill before the National Assembly on applying the AI Act.

updates.summary: Amendment of Act 56/2018 on product conformity assessment and eight other acts that adapts Slovak law to EU product legislation, including the AI Act. It adds Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 to the EU acts under which the Slovak Office of Standards, Metrology and Testing acts as notifying authority, and requires authorised (notified) bodies to meet further duties under such acts, citing Articles 36 and 45 of the AI Act. The Office may fine an authorised body at the levels of Article 99(4) and (6) of the AI Act for breaching the obligations listed in Article 99(4)(f), and reports such fines to the Commission. It names no AI Act market surveillance authority, single point of contact or sandbox.
updates.notes: Approved by the National Council on 21 October 2025, promulgated in the Collection of Laws on 21 November 2025 and in force from 1 January 2026. Article I has 77 amending points; Articles II to IX amend the acts on administrative fees, maritime navigation, state control of the internal market in consumer protection, labour inspection, public health, hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment, cybersecurity and the accessibility of products and services. Only its AI Act provisions are summarised here. The AI Act appears in the footnote to section 3(2) of Act 56/2018, which makes the Office the notifying authority under the act and under the EU acts listed there. The pending government bill SK-02 would name the Office as the AI Act's notifying authority and designate the other AI Act authorities.
updates.scope_note: Omnibus amendment of the conformity-assessment act; included because it adds Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 to the notified-body regime and sets fines under Article 99 of the AI Act.

updates.summary: Non-binding guidelines adopted by Government Conclusion on 23 March 2023 as a preventive mechanism for checking that machine-learning systems meet the highest ethical and security standards. The Government recommends that state, provincial and local bodies, public institutions and enterprises, regulators and holders of public powers apply them to the AI systems they set up and use, and other developers and users too. It defines AI systems and high-risk AI systems, lists high-risk areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure and law enforcement, and sets four principles and seven conditions for reliable and responsible AI, with recommendations and an assessment questionnaire.
updates.notes: The four principles are explainability and verifiability, dignity, prohibition of harm and fairness. The seven conditions are agency and oversight; technical reliability and safety; privacy, personal data protection and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and equality; social and environmental well-being; and accountability. The guidelines rest on the AI Development Strategy for 2020-2025 (Službeni glasnik RS 96/2019), one of whose five goals is ethical and safe AI, and its Action Plan for 2020-2022 (Službeni glasnik RS 81/2020), and draw on the 2021 UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI and the European Commission's April 2021 AI Act proposal. The competent minister determines how their application is integrated. They do not cover systems prohibited by a law regulating AI, and they record that AI needs to be regulated by law. The text is dated February 2023.

updates.summary: National AI strategy for 2025–2028, approved by presidential order on 19 March 2025. Its first priority direction is AI governance: identifying national priority sectors and responsible state bodies, a normative legal framework for responsible and ethical AI, rules to identify and prevent personal-data risks in AI systems, and AI standards. Its goals include legal norms and ethical rules for AI, responsible use that protects citizens' rights and data privacy, preventing data bias and use against the interests of the state, society and citizens, reducing the risks of innovative solutions, and protecting national and information security against manipulation and disinformation.
updates.notes: The order makes the Cabinet of Ministers coordinate and supervise the strategy's measures and report to the President once a year, tasks the State Service for Special Communications and Information Security with analysing information-security risks where state bodies use AI, and has the Center for Analysis of Economic Reforms and Communication monitor and evaluate implementation on the Cabinet's commission. The action plan (section 8) gives the Cabinet, with the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport and other bodies, 2025–2027 to create a normative legal framework for responsible and ethical AI (measure 8.1.3) and to approve rules on identifying and preventing personal-data risks in AI systems (8.1.4), and 2025–2026 to identify national priority sectors for AI and the responsible state bodies (8.1.1). By Order No. 253s of 28 April 2025 the Cabinet asked the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport to submit proposals on measure 8.1.1 by 1 July 2026 and on measures 8.1.3 and 8.1.4 by 1 July 2027, had the Center build a module for monitoring and reporting on the strategy, and set up a working group led by the head of the Cabinet's Office. By Decision No. 226 of 21 July 2026 the Cabinet approved the list of national priority sectors for AI development and the responsible state bodies. A presidential decree of 27 February 2026 created a Digital Development Council, chaired by the First Vice-President, to oversee state programmes and coordinate policy in digitalisation, e-government, AI and innovation and to take measures to improve the legislation.
updates.scope_note: Mainly a strategy for AI industry, skills, data and computing infrastructure and public-sector use; included because its first priority direction is AI governance, with a legal framework for responsible and ethical AI and rules on personal-data risks.
